precepts.text: The fear of the Lord is all wisdom, and in all wisdom is the performance of the law: acceptable faithfulness.
precepts.point: If thou wilt, to keep the commandments and to perform acceptable faithfulness: keeping the commandments is performing faithfulness, so your works prove your faith and your faith proves your works. That was what the last class left out for the commenters.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Works Of The Law & Liberty

precepts.why:
Sirach 15:15 says, “If thou wilt, to keep the commandments, and to perform acceptable faithfulness.” Keeping God's commandments is performing acceptable faithfulness: those are your actions, and that is where your faith lies. Your works prove your faith and your faith proves your works; they go hand in hand. God “hath set fire and water before thee: stretch forth thy hand unto whether thou wilt.”

For anyone still confused, Sirach 19:20 says it again: “The fear of the Lord is all wisdom; and in all wisdom is the performance of the law, and the knowledge of his omnipotency.” The performance of the law is the acceptable faithfulness of Sirach 15. Wisdom is not only knowing the law; it is performing it.

The words “the knowledge of his omnipotency” mean knowing that God is all around us, and we acknowledge it by keeping his laws.

This is what Habakkuk and Paul mean by the just living by faith. Paul says “the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” The just are those who keep God's laws and commandments, and they live by faith in Christ. Fearing God, keeping his law and living by faith are one walk.

precepts.text: Because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes and my laws: past tense, what he was doing that proved his faith.
precepts.point: If thou wilt, to keep the commandments and to perform acceptable faithfulness: keeping the commandments is performing faithfulness, so your works prove your faith and your faith proves your works. That was what the last class left out for the commenters.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Works Of The Law & Liberty

precepts.why:
God told Isaac why the promise stood: “Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” Abraham obeyed, and he kept the charge, the commandments, the statutes and the laws. That is past tense. It tells you what Abraham was doing from the beginning that proved his faith. His obedience was his acceptable faithfulness, the performance of Sirach 15:15.

Paul writes, “And the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them.” The law meant there is the law of sacrifice, which came later. Abraham's faith came first, and his faith and the promise to him go hand in hand; the promise predates the law of sacrifice.

“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us”. The curse of the law is condemnation, not being able to atone for every sin. Caiaphas pointed it out without knowing it: “it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.” Both the northern and southern kingdoms were under the old covenant they agreed to in Deuteronomy 27 and kept breaking, so both were condemned and destroyed by the nations. But the Lord loved them, sent his son to die for them, and took them out of that contract into a new one, “That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ”, meaning the northern kingdom.

Paul says “before faith came, we were kept under the law”, and “the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” The schoolmaster is the law of sacrifice, and the “we” is Israel. After faith came, “we are no longer under a schoolmaster.” Jews, Greeks, bond, free, male and female were all the same people of God in Christ.

“And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” Abraham is the father of faith, so his children should be children of faith like him: keeping the commandments the way he did, with faith in Christ instead of the animal sacrifice the Galatians were bewitched back into. The promise pertains to the Israelites, not to all nations.

precepts.text: The Most High has commanded no man to do wickedly and has given no man licence to sin, so whatever you are going through does not give you the right to sin.
precepts.point: Stand in awe, and sin not; commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah. Be angry but sin not; no matter what you are going through, the Most High does not give you the right to sin.

note.label: Psalm 4: The Lord Hath Set Apart Him That Is Godly for Himself

precepts.why:
“Stand in awe, and sin not”. Be angry, but sin not. Ecclesiasticus closes the door on every excuse: “He hath commanded no man to do wickedly, neither hath he given any man licence to sin.” The Most High has commanded no man to do wickedly and has given no man licence to sin, so whatever you are going through does not give you the right to sin.

Instead, “commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still.” No matter what you are going through, the Most High has not given you the right to sin.

precepts.text: He hath commanded no man to do wickedly, neither hath He given any man license to sin.
precepts.point: There is no sin in the Most High. Our people may struggle saying you cannot keep all the laws, but the Most High says His laws are not grievous and He did not give any man permission to sin.

note.label: Psalm 92: Planted in the House of the Lord

precepts.why:
There is no unrighteousness in the Most High, and he gives none to us either. “He hath commanded no man to do wickedly, neither hath he given any man licence to sin.”

Our people may struggle, saying you cannot keep all the laws, but the Most High says his laws are not grievous, and he did not give any man permission to sin. He commanded no man to do wickedly.

So those planted in his house are to be fat and flourishing in righteousness even in old age, to show that the Lord is upright. If there is no unrighteousness in him and no licence to sin from him, then keeping his law is what shows he is our rock.

precepts.text: The Most High hates all abomination, and they that fear Him love it not.
precepts.point: They served idols, sacrificed their sons and daughters to devils, and shed innocent blood, polluting the land and going a-whoring with their own inventions.

note.label: Psalm 106: Israel's Rebellions and the Mercy That Gathers Them Again

precepts.why:
“The Lord hateth all abomination; and they that fear God love it not.” The sacrifices of sons and daughters unto devils, the idols of Canaan, the whoring with their own inventions: these are the abominations he hates.

They that fear him love none of it. Israel was defiled with their own works because they learned to love what the Most High hates.

precepts.point: The Most High taketh pleasure in them that fear Him and in those that hope in His mercy. We are still talking about Israel here. He takes pleasure in those that fear Him, meaning those that keep His commandments. The way we know what fear is comes through the precepts.

note.label: Psalm 147: The Most High Gathers the Outcasts of Israel

precepts.why: “He that feareth the Lord will do good, and he that hath the knowledge of the law shall obtain her.” This is what it is to fear him: he that feareth the Lord will do good, keeping his commandments. The Most High taketh pleasure in them that fear him, and we know what that fear is through the precepts. You hope in his mercy and you keep his commandments, because faith without works is dead.

precepts.text: The Most High commanded no man to do wickedly, nor gave any man a licence to sin.
precepts.point: The witness under Christ is not two or three men but the Most High himself and the angels who always behold his face, so nothing is hidden from him.

note.label: Acts 5: All Things Common, and We Ought to Obey God Rather Than Men

precepts.why:
“He hath commanded no man to do wickedly, neither hath he given any man licence to sin.”

Sapphira shared her husband's fate because they agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Most High. A wife submits to her husband as unto the Most High, in righteousness, not in wickedness; if he tells her to break the law, she is not to agree with him, because no man has been given licence to sin. A wife is meant to be a tower against death and a help meet. Had she refused the evil or brought it to the leadership, she could have saved his life, as Abigail did.
